q: what is asthma
what is airway hyper-responsiveness
why is it hard to breathe out in asthma
x:
Asthma is a long-term inflammation of the airways with airflow blockage that can reverse, either by itself or with a bronchodilator. People struggle most to get air out, so air gets trapped and the lungs over-inflate. The airways are also over-reactive: a trigger that a normal airway ignores makes them clamp down hard. The more reactive they are, the more often symptoms show up.

Severity rarely changes over a person's life. Mild asthma rarely becomes severe, and severe asthma is usually severe from the start.

q: what is the difference between extrinsic and intrinsic asthma
what is the atopic triad
why do nasal polyps matter in asthma
x: Extrinsic asthma is the allergic kind and the most common. Allergens like dust mites trigger it, and it often comes with allergic rhinitis and eczema (the atopic triad). Intrinsic asthma is the non-allergic kind, about 1 in 10. It starts in adulthood, skin tests are negative, immunoglobulin E is normal, nasal polyps are common, and it may be aspirin sensitive. It tends to be more severe and persistent. Under the microscope the disease is the same in both.

t: Classifying asthma severity from a description
q: how do I classify asthma severity
what is moderate persistent asthma
what if features fall in different categories
x:
You sort a patient by symptoms, night waking, rescue inhaler use, activity limits and lung function (for ages 12 and up). Intermittent follows a rule of twos: 2 or fewer days a week and 2 or fewer nights a month. Mild persistent is more than 2 days a week but not daily, with 3 to 4 nights a month and a 1-second volume above 80%. Moderate is daily symptoms, waking more than once a week but not nightly, and a 1-second volume of 60% to 80%. Severe is all-day symptoms, waking nearly every night, and a 1-second volume below 60%.

The key rule: the patient gets the most severe category in which any one feature falls. Two or more steroid courses in a year also count as persistent.

q: what do the asthma zones mean
what should I do in the yellow zone
what are the danger signs in asthma
x: The plan uses your personal best peak flow. Green (80% or more of your best, no symptoms) means take your daily controller. Yellow (50% to 79%, or cough, wheeze, night waking) means asthma is getting worse: add your quick-relief medicine and keep taking the controller. Red (under 50%, very short of breath, or quick-relief not helping) is a medical alert. Trouble walking or talking, or blue lips or fingernails, means get help now.

q: when do I measure peak flow
what does a 20% change in peak flow mean
x: First you use the meter to find your personal best when well. Then you measure each morning before your bronchodilator and each afternoon after it. A change of 20% or more between those two readings, or from day to day, means your asthma is poorly controlled.

t: Testing for asthma: spirometry and other tests
q: how is asthma diagnosed
what is a positive bronchodilator response
when is a provocation test not done
x: Spirometry before and after a short-acting bronchodilator is the main test. Asthma shows a low 1-second volume and ratio that improve by 12% or more after the bronchodilator. If spirometry is normal but asthma is suspected, a methacholine or histamine challenge can provoke the narrowing, but it is not done if the 1-second volume is already under 65% of predicted. An exercise challenge is used when exercise-induced symptoms are suspected. Allergy testing finds triggers, and exhaled nitric oxide shows airway inflammation.

q: why use an inhaled steroid for asthma
how do I avoid thrush
how long does an inhaled steroid take to work
x: Inhaled corticosteroids are the preferred first-line daily medicine for persistent asthma. They calm the airway inflammation, but the full effect can take months, so patients should not stop early. They can cause hoarseness, cough and oral thrush; using a spacer and rinsing and spitting after each dose lowers that risk. A rescue inhaler does not replace them, because they are controllers, not quick relief.

q: can I use a long-acting beta agonist alone
why combine it with an inhaled steroid
x: A long-acting beta-2 agonist opens the airways for up to 12 hours but does nothing about inflammation, so it must not be used alone. It is added to an inhaled corticosteroid, which may even let you use less steroid. Side effects are tremor and palpitations.

t: Aspirin-sensitive asthma and which drugs to avoid
q: which pain relievers are safe in asthma
why avoid beta blockers in asthma
what is aspirin-sensitive asthma
x: About 1 to 5% of people with asthma get worse after aspirin, anywhere from minutes to 12 hours later, with a runny nose, red eyes, facial flushing and wheeze. They should avoid the non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs (ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, indomethacin). The selective ones (celecoxib, meloxicam) can be used. Beta blockers should also be avoided in asthma because they can tighten the airways.

q: what is exercise-induced bronchospasm
how do I prevent it
how long does it last
x: This is airway narrowing brought on by exercise, common in children and adolescents. It starts during or within 3 minutes after exercise, peaks at 10 to 15 minutes and is gone by 60 minutes. A short-acting beta-2 agonist before exercise prevents it; regular inhaled corticosteroid use prevents it best. Cromolyn and leukotriene modifiers can also help, but cromolyn only works if taken beforehand.

q: why is my asthma not controlled
what is refractory asthma
x: The most common reason asthma stays out of control is not taking the medicine correctly or regularly (cost and misunderstanding are common reasons), so check compliance and technique first. True steroid-resistant asthma is very uncommon. Refractory asthma means persistent symptoms with poor lung function, or normal lung function with severe exacerbations; specialists may use monoclonal antibody drugs, which reduce the need for corticosteroids.
